snippet.title: The Canal That Cut Greece in Half
snippet.description:
Stretching through solid rock, the Corinth Canal is one of Greece’s most impressive engineering achievements. 🇬🇷

For thousands of years, rulers, emperors, and engineers dreamed of cutting a passage through the narrow Isthmus of Corinth to connect the Aegean Sea and the Ionian Sea. ⚓

When the canal was finally completed in the 19th century, it transformed travel and created a dramatic gateway into the Peloponnese, the legendary peninsula that was home to ancient Sparta, Olympia, Corinth, and some of the most important chapters of Greek history. 🏛️

Standing at its edge, you're not just looking at a canal—you're looking at the entrance to one of the most historic regions on Earth.

snippet.title: American Revolution: Road to Independence
snippet.description:
From a dispute over taxes to a fight for the soul of a nation — the American Revolution begins here.

In 1763, Britain stands at the peak of its power, master of a global empire. Yet within a decade, some of its most prosperous colonies will be in open revolt. Our documentary covers the road to America's Declaration of Independence — from the first stirrings of colonial defiance to the moment the rebellion threatened to engulf the world.

We follow the escalating clash between a Parliament determined to assert its authority and colonists who refuse to be governed without consent. We witness the spark that ignites open warfare, the formation of a ragged Continental Army, and the emergence of the leaders — Washington, Adams, Franklin, and others — who will define a nation.

Along the way: celebrated battles, catastrophic defeats, desperate retreats, and moments of extraordinary courage. And through it all, the slow, painful realisation on both sides that there may be no going back.

By 1776, the thirteen colonies have declared independence, and Britain's imperial rivals are beginning to take notice. The colonial revolution is becoming a global war.

snippet.title: The Arabs - From Desert Tribes to a World Empire | 4K Documentary
snippet.description:
The Arab Golden Age was one of the most influential periods in world history – yet it remains largely forgotten in the West. From the 8th to the 13th century, the Arab Empire stretched from Spain to the borders of China, larger than Rome at its peak. 

In its capital Baghdad, Caliph Al-Mamun founded the House of Wisdom, where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars translated and expanded the knowledge of the ancient Greeks, Persians, and Indians. This documentary explores the rise of Islam under the Prophet Muhammad, the rapid Arab conquests across three continents, and the scientific revolution that followed in Baghdad and Moorish Spain. 

Discover how Persian mathematician Al-Khwarizmi invented algebra and gave us the word "algorithm", how surgeon Al-Zahrawi (Abulcasis) pioneered modern surgery in Córdoba, and how the musician Ziryab transformed European fashion, dining, and music – including the invention of the guitar. 

Without the Arab world, there would be no algebra, no decimal system, no Arabic numerals, no modern medicine as we know it. The translation movement in Toledo brought this knowledge to Europe and laid the foundation for the Renaissance, influencing thinkers from Copernicus to Fibonacci. A story of science, culture, conquest, and a forgotten legacy that shaped the modern world.

snippet.title: How Christianity Exploded Across the World
snippet.description:
How did Christianity spread so dramatically across the globe during the 19th and 20th centuries? 

In this short, we explore the age of missionaries, when Christian preachers, teachers, doctors, and explorers carried their faith into Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and beyond. This was one of the most important eras in the global history of Christianity.

During the missionary age, churches sent thousands of missionaries overseas, often building schools, hospitals, printing presses, and new religious communities. Bible translations helped spread Christian teachings into local languages, while global empires, trade routes, and colonial expansion made long-distance missions easier than ever before. But this story was not simple. The spread of Christianity was tied not only to faith and sacrifice, but also to power, empire, and cultural conflict.

This video looks at how missionaries helped Christianity grow into a truly global religion during the 19th and 20th centuries, transforming societies and leaving a legacy that is still debated today. From conversion and education to controversy and resistance, the missionary age changed world history forever.

snippet.title: The Tragic People's Crusade: Looting, Massacres, and Total Defeat
snippet.description:
What happens when religious zeal outruns discipline, strategy, and leadership? In this short, we explore the tragic story of the People’s Crusade, the chaotic and disastrous popular movement that marched east before the main armies of the First Crusade. Driven by faith, desperation, and fiery preaching, thousands of peasants, pilgrims, and poorly armed followers set out for Jerusalem—but many never came close.

Led in part by Peter the Hermit, the People’s Crusade was marked from the beginning by disorder, hunger, and violence. As these uncontrolled bands crossed Europe, some turned to looting, while others carried out horrific massacres of Jewish communities in the Rhineland, leaving a dark stain on crusading history. Lacking supplies, discipline, and real military organization, the movement became as dangerous to civilians as it was vulnerable to its enemies.

When the crusaders finally reached Byzantine territory and crossed into Anatolia, their weaknesses were exposed. Facing the experienced Seljuk Turks, the People’s Crusade collapsed in catastrophe, especially at the Battle of Civetot in 1096, where much of the force was destroyed. What began as a wave of religious enthusiasm ended in slaughter and defeat.

This is the story of one of medieval history’s most tragic campaigns—a warning about fanaticism, poor leadership, and mob violence. If you enjoy powerful stories from the Crusades and the turning points of history, subscribe to Epic History for more history shorts.

Facing the experienced Seljuk Turks, the People’s Crusade collapsed in catastrophe, especially at the Battle of Civetot in 1096, where much of the force was destroyed. What began as a wave of religious enthusiasm ended in slaughter and defeat.

This is the story of one of medieval history’s most tragic campaigns—a warning about fanaticism, poor leadership, and mob violence. If you enjoy powerful stories from the Crusades and the turning points of history, subscribe to Epic History for more history shorts.

snippet.title: Benedict Arnold’s Disastrous March to Quebec
snippet.description:
What kind of man marches an army through freezing wilderness, starving, sick, and dying—just for one desperate chance at victory? 

Before Benedict Arnold became America’s most infamous traitor, he was one of its boldest commanders. In 1775, Arnold led a brutal expedition through the wilds of Maine toward Quebec in one of the most desperate missions of the American Revolution.

His men faced freezing rain, deep mud, starvation, disease, and total exhaustion. Supplies rotted, boats failed, and soldiers collapsed as the wilderness swallowed the army step by step. Yet Arnold kept pushing forward, driven by the dream of striking the British by surprise and bringing Canada into the Revolution.

By the time they reached Quebec, the force was shattered—but the assault still came. What followed was a dramatic attack filled with chaos, courage, and disaster. Arnold was wounded, the assault failed, and the campaign ended in defeat. But the march itself became legendary: a story of endurance, ambition, and the terrifying cost of war.

This YouTube Short explores Benedict Arnold’s treacherous march to Quebec, one of the harshest military expeditions in early American history. If you love epic history, forgotten battles, and dramatic true stories from the American Revolution, this is for you.
